title: Pea and Ham Soup
subtitle: Thick split-pea broth with a ham hock
excerpt: Split peas simmered with a whole ham hock until both are tender, the peas collapsing into a thick, deeply savoury broth. The hock shreds back in at the end. One of the best soups to make on a cold weekend.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pea and ham soup is one of the oldest British soup traditions, appearing in various forms in medieval cookery. The core technique is to simmer a smoked pork knuckle or ham hock with split peas until both the peas and the pork are completely soft. The peas dissolve into the stock, thickening it naturally. The smoky depth from the ham hock is the key flavour. Green split peas produce a greener soup; yellow split peas a mellower one. Both work equally well.

recipeTools.notes: Large pot for the ham hock and peas.

content.text: Split peas do not need soaking overnight. Rinse them and add them directly to the pot with the hock. The peas will absorb the smoky, salty liquid from the hock as they cook, building the flavour without additional seasoning until the end. Taste before adding salt: the hock is cured and can be very salty.
Put the ham hock in a large pot. Cover with cold water and bring to the boil. Discard the water. This removes excess salt from the cure. Rinse the pot.

Return the hock to the pot. Add the split peas, onion, carrot, celery, garlic, bay leaves, and thyme. Cover with 2 litres of cold water. Bring to a gentle simmer. Skim any scum from the surface. Cook uncovered for 2 to 2.5 hours, stirring occasionally, until the peas have dissolved into the soup and the pork is falling off the bone.
Remove the ham hock and set aside to cool slightly. Pull the meat from the bone and shred into pieces. Discard the bone and excess fat. Fish out the bay leaves and thyme stalks.

If the soup is too thick, add a splash of water and stir. Taste carefully before seasoning with salt: the hock may have provided enough. Add pepper. Stir the shredded ham back into the soup. Serve hot with crusty bread, scattered with parsley.
